# Operational handover

<!-- Generated from register.md by the register drift gate (ADR-069; T-BLD-006). Do not edit: amend register.md by ID, then regenerate. -->

## Deployment assumption

**No real deployment of this build exists.** The application runs as two localhost origins over plain HTTP, and
every production-only value is asserted by test and never executed. Two things follow, and a reader must not
mistake either for an omission:

- A row whose `responsibility` is `none` has no `priority`. That is the schema, not a gap.
- Limitation rows (`sequence` `L`) state what nobody can currently prove. On the first real deployment their
  `responsibility` becomes `deployer`, they gain a `priority`, and the table is regraded.

## 2. Trusted-proxy configuration

| ID | what to do | responsibility | priority | status | how to prove it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <a id="r-rl-005"></a>R-RL-005 | Every limiter is in memory, in one instance, and keyed per source key, submitted username or identifier. There is no global bulkhead, so aggregate BCrypt CPU and request-thread occupancy grow with the number of sources. The request thread pool is pinned by `server.tomcat.threads.max`, and Tomcat and Hikari saturation meters are exposed. | shared | required | asserted-by-test | The pinned thread value is recorded against the deployed instance size, and T-OBS-005 shows both saturation meters non-zero after a password path is exercised. |
| <a id="r-rl-007"></a>R-RL-007 | The application binds `app.security.client-ip.source` (`socket` by default, or `proxy`) and `app.security.client-ip.trusted-proxies`, which has no default. Selecting `proxy` without an explicit list fails context refresh, and Tomcat's `internal-proxies` and `forward-headers-strategy` are both derived from that one input; the deployer names the proxy addresses. | shared | blocking | asserted-by-test | T-CFG-001, T-CFG-025 and T-CFG-026 pass; inspection shows the deployed trusted-proxies value lists exactly the proxies in front of the application, and a request through the proxy is keyed on the client's address. |
| <a id="r-rl-010"></a>R-RL-010 | Row 5 DISK_RESERVE_SHED is a per-event alert, and while shedding lasts admins without a live session cannot log in. It clears on its own within about W + 60 s + D of the attack stopping; a restart does not clear it and leaves the episode without a clearing row; Retry-After: 60 is the earliest possible clear. While the attack continues, the only remedy is the edge per-source limit, which must aggregate IPv6 at a deployer-chosen prefix. | deployer | required | asserted-by-test | The runbook names row 5 DISK_RESERVE_SHED, the self-clearing bound and the edge per-source limit (keyed on a chosen IPv6 prefix) as the remedy; T-RL-024 and T-AUD-039 pass. |
| <a id="r-rl-023"></a>R-RL-023 | A user population known to sit on /56 prefixes reopens the declined second /56 key. | deployer | recommended | procedural | The deployer's declaration of its user networks records whether /56 assignment dominates. |
| <a id="r-obs-015"></a>R-OBS-015 | A servlet filter at the highest precedence strips every caller-supplied trace-context header (traceparent, tracestate, b3, the five X-B3 headers, baggage, plus the propagators' own fields read at startup), so trace.id is a server-generated 128-bit value on every request. A deployer who fronts the application with a tracing gateway will see traces never continue; the fix is a new trusted-boundary decision, not a configuration change or removing the wrapper. | deployer | recommended | asserted-by-test | An inbound traceparent never matches the logged trace.id: T-OBS-002 and T-OBS-003 pass, and the deployed configuration leaves the strip wrapper and propagation settings unchanged. |
| <a id="r-ops-006"></a>R-OPS-006 | The per-source budget table is a request-rate allowlist: routes absent from it are not rate-limited by the application, and raw request rate on them is bounded by an edge or ingress policy the deployer owns. The application meters session-store misses on every route instead. | deployer | required | unmitigated | A documented edge or ingress policy names a per-source request ceiling, keys IPv6 on a chosen prefix, and is shown applied to paths outside the budget table. |
| <a id="r-ops-008"></a>R-OPS-008 | State whether IPv6 clients reach the public endpoint natively, and re-declare whenever the edge or DNS changes. | deployer | required | procedural | An AAAA lookup on the public name, recorded beside the startup log line that states the IPv6 prefix length. |
| <a id="r-ops-010"></a>R-OPS-010 | In proxy mode the trusted proxy writes IP literals, never hostnames or obfuscated tokens, and the deployer alerts on `app.client_ip.unparseable` above zero. | deployer | required | asserted-by-test | The unparseable counter reads zero after a representative traffic sample through the edge. |

## 7. Recovery rehearsal

| ID | what to do | responsibility | priority | status | how to prove it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <a id="r-lck-003"></a>R-LCK-003 | ASVS 6.1.1 is graded pass-with-note pending the first recovery rehearsal. Its final clause, that the documentation make clear how the controls "prevent malicious account lockout", passes only because the escalating 20/40/60-minute lockout ladder and the offline rebinding runner both exist. | shared | blocking | asserted-by-test | The first recovery rehearsal on the deployed topology passes; T-LCK-010, T-LCK-011 and T-RUN-009 pass; the documentation quotes the "prevent malicious account lockout" clause. |
| <a id="r-lck-009"></a>R-LCK-009 | Per-account lockout auto-expires: the password ladder locks for 20, then 40, then 60 minutes, and the TOTP tier-1 lock lasts 20 minutes. An admin cannot unlock their own account, by design, but is delayed rather than locked out. The runbook says so, and warns that "wait twenty minutes" is wrong advice for an account under sustained attack, whose lock escalates. | deployer | recommended | procedural | Inspection: the runbook states the ladder durations and the TOTP tier-1 duration beside the lockout scenario, and forbids direct database edits for a lockout. |
| <a id="r-lck-010"></a>R-LCK-010 | Issuing a reset token as an admin clears neither the password lockout nor the failed-attempt cap. Both clear when the user redeems the token; an admin may instead unlock through the audited unlock endpoint with reason `PASSWORD_RESET_COMPLETED`. Support is told that a lingering lock is not a failed reset. | shared | recommended | asserted-by-test | T-LCK-017 and T-CRED-024 pass; the support runbook states that a lock survives admin issuance and clears on redemption. |
| <a id="r-lck-011"></a>R-LCK-011 | The cap is implemented: 100 consecutive failures disable the password authenticator until rebinding. One host sustains about 36 disables per hour; the per-source cardinality axis cuts that about 100× per bucket, but the ladder binds from about 20 source keys, which IPv6 makes free for anyone holding more than one /64. The ladder gives about 9.7 h between alert and permanence, with the cap at about 14 h. | shared | required | asserted-by-test | T-LCK-016, T-LCK-020, T-LCK-011 and T-RL-006 pass; the alert fires in the consumer at the warning threshold; the deployer holds a costed recovery plan or signed acceptance for a mass-disable event. |
| <a id="r-lck-012"></a>R-LCK-012 | On the alert at 50 consecutive failures, act within about 9.7 h, in order: block the attacking prefixes at the edge, found by the exact HMAC join where the operator holds `app.security.hmac.log.key` and by timestamp otherwise; the owner signing in between locks, which is unreliable; the owner's own reset, unavailable outside `dev` until a mail transport exists. Name who holds the log key, and state that in this build every disable needs the rebinding runner. | shared | required | asserted-by-test | The runbook names the three routes, the log-key holder and the rebinding runner, and a dry run matches one known edge-log address to its `source.ip_hash`. |
| <a id="r-cred-006"></a>R-CRED-006 | The context-term check is built: username, email local-part and service name go to the strength estimator as user inputs, rejected as CONTEXT_TERM. ## L. Limitations: what nobody can currently prove

| ID | what to do | responsibility | priority | status | how to prove it |

| <a id="r-lck-005"></a>R-LCK-005 | About 100 unauthenticated requests permanently disable one account's password authenticator. The residual is 36 disables an hour from one unlimited source, about 0.36 an hour per limited source bucket, and never faster than about 14 hours per account, whatever the source count. | none |  | asserted-by-test | T-LCK-011, T-LCK-016 and T-LCK-020 pass (startup floor, cap binding, no disable before 840 minutes with the alert first). |
| <a id="r-rl-002"></a>R-RL-002 | The third limiter axis refuses a source key once it has driven k = 5 distinct accounts into lockout, each counted for an hour from its first lock. It is keyed on attacker-chosen source, so rotating source keys restores throughput, and the lockout ladder is then the bound. | none |  | asserted-by-test | T-RL-006, T-RL-007, T-RL-008 and T-RL-026 pass; no runtime evidence can bound the attacker's source count. |
| <a id="r-rl-003"></a>R-RL-003 | A full per-source set refuses only usernames that are not already members, and each member's expiry runs from its first insertion, so a refusal lasts about an hour after the fifth first lock. | none |  | asserted-by-test | T-RL-030 and T-RL-031 pass. |
| <a id="r-rl-006"></a>R-RL-006 | Rate limiters and session state are not shared across instances; the build supports exactly one instance, and a single-instance check at startup holds it. The prescribed distributed-consistency test is not run. | none |  | enforced | Inspection: the startup single-instance check exists and a second instance against the same database refuses to start. |
| <a id="r-rl-011"></a>R-RL-011 | The count line sheds new anonymous sessions at N_max = 100,000 live rows, so about 196 source keys at 510 rows each deny every new login regardless of volume size. Under /64 source keying that takes 196 LANs rather than one host; the cheapest supply is one AWS VPC or a residential /56. | none |  | asserted-by-test | T-RL-024 passes (the count line trips and clears with its band and dwell). |
| <a id="r-rl-012"></a>R-RL-012 | The free-space reserve uses b = 17 KB per row, read after CHECKPOINT at 100,000 rows, and k = 1.5, a judgement meant to cover the transient during a bulk DELETE. That DELETE peak was never sampled. | none |  | procedural | Inspection: the sizing line and ADR-041 state k and b as planning values; a sampled DELETE-peak measurement, when made, replaces k. |
| <a id="r-aud-009"></a>R-AUD-009 | State-changing audit rows are emitted after commit by a synchronous listener; a write failure after commit is caught and alerted (degraded row, ERROR, Logback status listener). A process crash between commit and write loses the row with no alert. | none |  | unmitigated | Inspection: rows are emitted after commit; T-AUD-031 shows write failures alert; the crash window itself cannot be tested closed. |
| <a id="r-aud-021"></a>R-AUD-021 | `source.ip_hash` is HMAC-SHA-256 under the log key over the prefix `ip:` and the source key, which aggregates IPv6 to a /64 by one property; an unparseable client token hashes a constant. | none |  | unmitigated | T-AUD-041 pins the hash input; inspection that any prefix-length change is logged in the change record. |
| <a id="r-aud-026"></a>R-AUD-026 | Logging throughput under expected load is not measured. Appenders are synchronous, to stdout and a rolling local file, so no event is dropped by design. | none |  | unmitigated | None obtainable in this build; a load test on a real deployment showing no dropped audit lines and acceptable latency discharges it. |

The SPA clears its own state unconditionally on sign-out, which is the real control. | none |  | asserted-by-test | T-HDR-005 passes in Chromium and Firefox, and T-FE-017 passes. |
